title: SYSK Live: The Kellogg Brothers’ Wacky World of Health
summary: A live Stuff You Should Know show recorded in Sydney, Australia, telling the story of brothers John Harvey Kellogg and Will Keith Kellogg. The episode opens with a mock time trip to 1876 America to describe the heavy, rich diets of the era, including a Delmonico's dinner. It covers the Seventh-day Adventist church and its Millerite roots, the Whites and their health reform ideas, and the founding of the Battle Creek Sanitarium, where John Harvey treated patients with exercise, diet, and unusual devices such as the kneading machine, electric light bath cabinet, and colonic machine, guided by the now-discredited theory of autointoxication. It discusses John Harvey's anti-tobacco and probiotic views alongside his extreme anti-masturbation remedies and eugenics, and the accidental invention of flaked cereal (corn flakes) at the sanitarium. Will later added sugar and salt, founded the Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company, and marketed heavily, including the New York Wink Wednesday campaign. The brothers fought lawsuits over the Kellogg name, and the episode closes with John Harvey's apology letter, which Will's secretary never mailed (per the hosts), and the brothers' gravesites in Oak Hill Cemetery. Includes two live-show ad/break segments with an audience member, Alex Sexton, who performed a jingle.

segments.title: Live show opening and 1876 time trip
segments.summary: The hosts open the live Sydney show and take the audience on a mock trip back to 1876 America to describe the heavy, multi-course diets of the era, including a Delmonico's dinner menu.

segments.title: Kellogg brothers' childhood and the Millerite roots of Adventism
segments.summary: John Harvey and Will Kellogg are introduced as health reformers raised in Battle Creek, Michigan, with a troubled older-brother relationship. The hosts then trace the Seventh-day Adventist Church from William Miller's failed predictions through the Great Disappointment to its reformation under Ellen White.

segments.title: Ellen White, health reform, and the Western Health Reform Institute
segments.summary: Ellen White linked religion to personal health and diet, and the church's leaders opened a health institute in Battle Creek modeled on James Caleb Jackson's New York spa; it failed at first. John Harvey was sent to medical school and returned in 1876 to run what became the Battle Creek Sanitarium.

segments.title: Battle Creek Sanitarium's growth and famous visitors
segments.summary: The sanitarium grew into a large luxury health resort with more than a thousand employees, and Will joined as head of human resources. Visitors included Amelia Earhart, William Howard Taft, Thomas Edison, and Johnny Weissmuller, while Middle America called the patients 'battle freaks.'

segments.title: Kellogg's bizarre treatments: kneading machine, light bath, colonic machine
segments.summary: John Harvey's treatments combined common-sense advice such as exercise, fresh air, and quitting smoking with odd devices like the kneading machine, electric light bath cabinet, and colonic machines. These were based on autointoxication, the discredited idea that trapped waste poisons the body. The hosts also describe his yogurt enema practice and his four-bowel-movements-a-day ideal.

segments.title: Live show break with Alex Sexton
segments.summary: A break in the live show, during which local audience member Alex Sexton comes on stage to perform a jingle he had written.

segments.title: John Harvey's anti-tobacco, probiotics, and food inventions
segments.summary: John Harvey wrote early against tobacco and promoted yogurt and probiotics, ideas ahead of his time. He is also credited as one of three inventors of peanut butter, developed nut-based meat substitutes, and created a caffeine-free coffee substitute.

segments.title: Kellogg's anti-masturbation remedies and eugenics
segments.summary: The hosts describe John Harvey's writings on masturbation in Plain Facts for the Old and Young, including a recommendation to circumcise boys without anesthetic, silver sutures to prevent erections, and a genital cage. They also cover his eugenics views, including a proposed pedigree registry and his 'Authentics' idea.
topics: Plain Facts for the Old and Young

segments.title: Invention of flaked cereal and granula lawsuit
segments.summary: Looking for an easy-to-digest breakfast, the brothers developed double-baked biscuits and then granula, copying James Caleb Jackson's recipe; Jackson sued, forcing a new recipe and name, granola. Grape-Nuts, later made by C. W. Post, came from this line of experiments. Corn dough left over from an experiment became tempered and rolled into flakes, and John Harvey took the patent alone.

segments.title: Live show break with Alex Sexton again
segments.summary: A second break in the live show, with Alex Sexton returning to the stage for another jingle performance with the audience.

segments.title: Sugar, salt, and Will's split with John Harvey
segments.summary: Will added sugar and salt to the corn flakes, which boosted sales. After John Harvey objected to a plant Will built while he was away, the brothers split. Will founded the Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company and bought the sweetened-flake patent. He then used the 'Wink Wednesday' advertising campaign in New York in 1906.
topics: Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company

segments.title: Corn flakes lawsuits, legacy, and nutrition critique
segments.summary: Will's company expanded to Canada and Australia and became a major cereal business, even during the Great Depression. John Harvey started a rival Kellogg's corn flakes product, and the brothers sued each other over the Kellogg name and rarely spoke again. The hosts note that modern nutritionists consider cereal, and the early refined flakes, less healthy because they removed fiber.

segments.title: John Harvey's later years, apology letter, and Battle Creek legacy
segments.summary: The sanitarium declined during the Depression and was sold to the US government as a military hospital. John Harvey grew eccentric in his final years, and in a late apology letter to Will he wrote that Will had been right in the food business; his secretary did not mail it. Will received the letter after John Harvey's death, and the W. K. Kellogg Foundation continues today.

segments.title: Oak Hill Cemetery gravesites and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts describe Will Kellogg's large burial plot in Oak Hill Cemetery in Battle Creek and note that John Harvey's original grave, about ten spots away, is still there. They close the show with a sign-off.
